Volume 10 · Chapter 03

Term-structure models and rate risk

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v10-c02

By the endCompare curve models and distinguish physical from risk-neutral dynamics.

A curve prices dated cash; a model prices changes in that curve

Capability. Compare curve models and distinguish physical from risk-neutral dynamics. Construct and calibrate a finite short-rate model, derive its pricing rules, measure conditional expected returns under a separate physical law, and identify which conclusions survive a different calibrated model. The prerequisite is Duration, convexity and immunization, including its explicit choice of curve-bump coordinates. We retain the dated discount factors of Bond cash flows and yield curves and the finite positive-state-price reasoning of Arbitrage pricing and stochastic discount factors. No stochastic differential equation or option-pricing theorem is assumed.

A treasury desk agrees on today's prices of one-, two- and three-year default-free zeros. Two analysts fit those prices exactly, yet quote different values for a payment linked to next year's bond price. A third reads the forward curve as a forecast of future policy rates. These disagreements concern different objects: today's dated prices, a pricing law for future states, and a physical forecast. A model review must keep all three visible.

All markets and data in this chapter are original synthetic teaching contracts, independent of the preceding chapters' numerical cases. Times 0, 1, 2 and 3 are annual dates. CU means currency units. A unit-face zero pays exactly 1 CU at its stated maturity. Rates are effective annual simple rates over a single annual interval, expressed as decimals. There is no default, tax, trading cost, collateral constraint or bid–ask spread. Signed bond and bank-account positions may be traded at the quoted prices; borrowing and lending use the same node rate. There is no separate right to store cash costlessly outside that account. This last assumption matters when a node rate is negative.

1. What is observed and what is added

Write DT = P(0;T) for today's price of a unit-face zero maturing at T, and D0 = 1. Our curve is D1 = 0.98, D2 = 0.95 and D3 = 0.91. It prices a fixed schedule CT by Σ CTDT. Its one-year forward rate for the interval from 1 to 2 is D1/D2 − 1 = 3/95. That rate is the price-implied borrowing/lending exchange between two dates, derived by zero-bond replication in Chapter 1.

Nothing in those three observations specifies how P(1;2) will vary across future states. A deterministic path of short rates can fit them; so can many stochastic paths. An interpolation between observed maturities answers a cross-sectional question about unobserved dates. A transition law answers a different question about future states and future curves. More densely interpolating today's curve supplies no additional history of changes in rates.

We distinguish the physical probability law ℙ, used for forecasts and expected realized returns, from the strictly positive conditional pricing law ℚ. The word risk-neutral describes a valuation representation relative to a chosen numeraire; it does not assert that actual investors are risk neutral. Our notation P(t,j;T) denotes a bond price, not either probability law. The information available at date t includes the branch history through that date.

2. A dated tree and its bank account

At date t, node j records the number of high-rate branches among the first t moves; j ranges from 0 through t. The node's short rate rt,j is known before investing over [t,t+1]. Define its discount dt,j = 1/(1+rt,j) > 0. A high branch increments j; a low branch leaves j unchanged. The probability of the high branch is qt,j under ℚ and pt,j under ℙ. Both lie strictly between zero and one. Consequently the two laws assign positive probability to the same finite path set.

Let A0 = 1 and At+1 = At/dt,j along each history. A is the value of one initial CU continually reinvested in the one-period bank account. The account's next growth factor is known at the current node, even though its growth over several future periods is random. Rates recombine by j in our model, but accumulated bank wealth need not: different histories can reach the same rate node after earning different earlier rates.

P(T,j;T) = 1.
P(t,j;T) = dt,j[(1−qt,j)P(t+1,j;T) + qt,jP(t+1,j+1;T)].

This recursion specifies model bond prices by backward valuation. For a security with an end-of-next-period cash payment Ct+1, put that payment inside the expectation along with its ex-payment continuation value. A coupon paid at t+1 must not be multiplied by an additional period's discount. For a terminal path payment H, repeated substitution yields:

Vt/At = Eℚ[H/AT | information at t].
V0 = Σpaths ℚ(path) H(path) ∏t=0T−1dt,j(path).

Discounting is inside the expectation because future short rates are random. Replacing the product by a discount calculated from an average short rate is a different operation. The backward recursion can be used for node-dependent payoffs; path-dependent payoffs require retaining the history needed to determine the payment.

Why these prices exclude an arbitrage within the stipulated market

For a zero-coupon asset before maturity, the pricing rule makes V/A a conditional ℚ-martingale: Eℚ[Vt+1/At+1|t] = Vt/At. Include a paid distribution in the next-period wealth when an asset distributes cash. At each date a trader selects holdings using information already available. Rebalancing is self-financing if the new holdings cost exactly the wealth released by the old holdings and their distributions; no outside money enters. Linearity and conditional expectation then give the same martingale equality for discounted self-financing wealth W/A, by induction over dates.

A strategy starting at W0 = 0 therefore has Eℚ[WT/AT] = 0. If WT were nonnegative on every physical path and positive on at least one, strict positive support and AT > 0 would make that expectation positive, a contradiction. Finite states and finite holdings make all expectations well defined here. An initially negative-cost arbitrage can be combined with a bank deposit to obtain the zero-cost form. This is an internal no-arbitrage result for the specified trading rights and consistently priced assets. It neither authenticates forecasts nor proves that every possible terminal claim is spanned by the traded bonds.

The accepted finite-state pricing source supports the positive-price and spanning distinction. Here the multi-date argument has been derived directly. Choosing a positive ℚ gives a consistent pricing extension; uniqueness requires additional traded payoffs and rank conditions.

3. Calibrate levels after specifying a shape and a pricing law

Let at,j be the date-0 price weight of reaching node (t,j), summing the discounted ℚ probabilities of its histories. Start with a0,0 = 1. Propagate weights forward:

at+1,j receives at,jdt,j(1−qt,j);
at+1,j+1 receives at,jdt,jqt,j.
ΣjaT,j = P(0;T).

Each path weight is its pricing probability divided by its bank-account value. The last equality prices the payoff of one in every state. The a weights are prices, not probabilities: their sum is DT, generally not one. Even after dividing by DT, their distribution is generally different from the distribution of nodes under the bank-account pricing law ℚ.

Our original calibration chooses q = 1/2 at every node and a nonnegative dispersion parameter s < 1/2. Define ht,j = 1+s(t−2j), for t = 0,1,2, and set dt,j = ctht,j. The restriction ensures every shape is positive; it is tailored to this three-period tree. Increasing j lowers the discount and raises the short rate. Given the already computed date-t Arrow weights, choose:

ct = Dt+1 / Σj=0tat,jht,j.

The denominator is positive. Substituting into the forward recursion gives Σat+1,j = ctΣat,jht,j = Dt+1. Thus each level fits its next maturity exactly, without disturbing earlier levels. This proves existence and uniqueness of the fitted level conditional on the chosen shape, conditional ℚ probabilities and earlier levels. It does not identify that shape or those probabilities from the curve. Any strictly positive discount curve is admissible under this algebra and the stated absence of external cash storage. Positive node discounts imply rates above −100%; they do not require rates to be nonnegative.

Haugh's Term Structure Lattice Models, selected finite-lattice sections, is the primary teaching route for backward bond pricing, forward state prices and sequential curve fitting. The discount-shape family and all cases here are original; they are not the source's Ho–Lee or Black–Derman–Toy parameterization.

Worked example 1 — One exact curve fit

Use s = 1/50 = 0.02. First c0 = 49/50, giving a1 = (49/100,49/100). At date 1 the shapes are 51/50 and 49/50, whose a-weighted sum is 49/50. Hence c1 = (19/20)/(49/50) = 95/98. Its node discounts are 969/980 and 19/20, and its short rates are 11/969 ≈ 1.13519% and 1/19 ≈ 5.26316%.

Base model: node values ordered from lowest to highest short rate
Date tLevel ctNode discounts for [t,t+1]Short rates, approximately
049/5049/502.04082%
195/98969/980; 19/201.13519%; 5.26316%
245500/4751947320/47519; 45500/47519; 43680/475190.42054%; 4.43736%; 8.78892%

The next Arrow row is a2 = (969/4000,19/40,931/4000) = (0.24225,0.475,0.23275). Its sum is 0.95. Multiplying that row by the date-2 shapes (26/25,1,24/25) gives 47519/50000, so c2 = (91/100)/(47519/50000) = 45500/47519. Forward propagation then gives total date-3 weight 0.91. Backward valuation independently gives the same three zero prices.

A separate bond pays 5 at date 1, 5 at date 2 and 105 at date 3. Its value is 5(0.98)+5(0.95)+105(0.91) = 105.20 CU. Backward valuation, adding each coupon once at its payment date, gives the same result. A successful fit guarantees these supplied fixed-payment prices. It does not yet validate the amount of future rate uncertainty.

4. Expectations, covariance and the meaning of a term premium

At a node, write d for the known one-period discount, and let pb and qb be physical and pricing probabilities for branch b. Define the local physical stochastic discount factor mb = d qb/pb. Both laws have positive support, so this ratio is finite and positive. For a next-period payment X:

Price = d Eℚ[X] = Eℙ[mX];   Eℙ[m] = d.
For a traded gross holding return G: Eℙ[mG] = 1.
Eℙ[G] − 1/d = −Covℙ(m,G)/d.

The last line follows by expanding the covariance. It identifies the expected excess return in this model, not a guaranteed realized excess return. A bond that pays relatively well in high-m states can have a negative expected excess return. The physical law, state prices and cash flows all matter. The pathwise SDF is the product of local m values, equal to the path price divided by its physical probability.

The curve-implied forward is also not generally the mean next short rate under ℚ. At date 0, d0 = D1 is known, and D2/D1 = Eℚ[1/(1+r1)]. Therefore:

1+f1,2 = 1 / Eℚ[1/(1+r1)] ≤ Eℚ[1+r1].
f1,2−Eℙ[r1] = (f1,2−Eℚ[r1]) + (Eℚ[r1]−Eℙ[r1]).

The inequality follows from convexity of 1/x on x > 0, or the harmonic–arithmetic mean inequality. It is strict when the next rate is nonconstant with positive probability. The first difference is a nonlinear averaging effect; the second reflects the difference between the two probability laws. Calling their sum a pure risk premium hides this distinction. A yield-minus-expected-average-rate measure has its own maturity and compounding convention; it must not be silently substituted for the one-period holding-return premium above.

Worked example 2 — Same prices, different physical expected returns

Keep the base model's ℚ probability of a high branch at 1/2. Specify physical high probability p0,0 = 7/10. Then Eℚ[r1] = 31/969 ≈ 3.19917%, while Eℙ[r1] = 13/323 ≈ 4.02477%. The forward is 3/95 ≈ 3.15789%. In decimal rate units, its gap from the physical forecast is −14/1615, decomposed into −2/4845 from nonlinear averaging and −8/969 from changing the probability law. These are supplied model quantities, not estimates extracted from market observations.

Buy one two-year zero for 0.95 at date 0 and sell it at date 1, before its maturity payment. Its possible sale values are 969/980 and 19/20. Dividing by its purchase price gives gross returns 51/49 and 1, hence simple returns 2/49 and 0. Its physical expected simple return is (3/10)(2/49) = 3/245 ≈ 1.22449%, below the bank rate 1/49 by 2/245 ≈ 0.81633 percentage points.

The local physical SDF is (49/30,7/10). Its mean is 49/50 and its covariance with the bond's gross return is 1/125. Thus −Cov(m,G)/d = −(1/125)/(49/50) = −2/245, matching the direct calculation. The low-rate state has both higher bond value and higher m; the bond provides valuable state-contingent insurance under this specified pricing relation.

To exhibit changing conditional premiums, specify physical high probabilities of 2/5 at the low date-1 node and 4/5 at the high date-1 node. For a date-3 zero held only from date 1 to date 2, the conditional expected excess returns are respectively 196/49419 ≈ 0.39661 percentage points and −12/931 ≈ −1.28894 percentage points. They are obtained from each node's own purchase price, possible next sale values and bank rate. Premiums can vary by date and state; an unchanged initial curve does not impose constant compensation for holding-period risk.

The Federal Reserve's methodological Q&A, updated 5 November 2019, distinguishes its reported expectations/term-premium decomposition from a separate pure-premium convention, and explains why fitting yields does not establish sensible expectations. It discusses persistence, finite histories and survey information as estimation issues. This is a dated methodological reference; we use no current yield observations or source numerical estimates.

5. Compare model families by their restrictions

A deterministic short-rate path sets dt = Dt+1/Dt. It reproduces every initial zero price, but has no future rate uncertainty. It is useful as a controlled comparison. Treating it as an empirical forecast requires evidence that a static curve does not supply.

A finite additive mean-reverting process instead specifies, under a named law, rn+1 = θ+φ(rn−θ)+σεn+1, with independent equiprobable ε = ±1, 0 ≤ φ < 1 and σ ≥ 0. Here θ is a long-run mean level, φ is persistence per step, and σ has rate units. Iterating the recursion gives:

rn = θ+φn(r0−θ)+σΣk=1nφn−kεk.
E[rn] = θ+φn(r0−θ).
Var(rn) = σ²Σk=0n−1φ2k = σ²(1−φ2n)/(1−φ²).

Independence and zero innovation means eliminate cross terms in the variance. The conditional mean moves toward θ, not necessarily every realized path. If φ = 1, the mean stays at the initial rate and variance is nσ²; that is a different, non-mean-reverting boundary. Negative additive rates are possible. Finite pricing use requires every reachable rate to exceed −1. The finite model alone supplies no theorem about unbounded continuous-time innovations.

For a separate physical example with θ = 0.02, φ = 1/2, σ = 0.01 and r0 = 0.08, the first future rates are 0.04 and 0.06. The four two-step rates are 0.02, 0.04, 0.03 and 0.05, each with probability 1/4. The mean is 0.035 and variance 0.000125. Distinct histories with one positive innovation need not recombine, because the earlier innovation is attenuated. This model is not automatically fitted to our curve. Calling its law ℙ or ℚ, estimating its parameters, and adding calibration shifts are separate decisions.

A positive-rate construction r = exp(x) restricts every short rate to be strictly positive. A positive-rate tree implies d < 1 at every node and therefore declining initial discounts: Dt+1 = Σat,jdt,j < Σat,j = Dt. It cannot fit an increasing discount segment without changing its structure, for example by admitting a shift that allows negative rates. Fitting a level while preserving a chosen positive-rate family may be impossible for a supplied curve.

In the inspected finite lattice material, Haugh contrasts additive rate levels with log-rate levels and calibrates them conditionally on dispersion choices. Our s controls a discount shape; it is not a universal volatility in rate units. Its economic meaning changes with the fitted level.

A proposed square-root-scaled finite update r′ = r+κ(θ−r)+σ√r ε illustrates a further trap. The square root in the formula does not guarantee nonnegative next rates. The down move can exceed the current rate plus drift. Replacing negative outcomes by zero changes the mean, variance and pricing recursion, so it requires explicit recalibration and a revised model description. Positivity properties of a continuous-time process cannot be assumed for a finite step merely because the formulas look related.

6. Exact curve fit can coexist with claim and hedge disagreement

For the three-period discount-shape family, set s = 0, 0.02 or 0.04 and recalibrate the levels in each case. Keep ℚ probabilities at one half and keep the same initial D. Every fixed-payment bond has the same initial price across these models. To expose the missing information, define a new contract: at date 1 it pays H = max(100P(1;2)−96,0) CU in cash, and then ends. This is a fully specified nonlinear payment based on the price of 100 CU face of the date-2 zero. There is no payment or purchase at date 2 under this contract. Its pricing and hedge follow from two elementary linear equations, which we now solve locally.

Worked example 3 — Price disagreement and a frozen hedge

Three exactly curve-calibrated models, same date-1 contingent payment rule
Dispersion sLow/high P(1;2)Low/high HDate-0 claim price
095/98; 95/9846/49; 46/490.92
0.02969/980; 19/20141/49; 01.41
0.04247/245; 228/245236/49; 02.36

Each claim price is 0.98 times the ℚ average of its two payoffs. In the deterministic case the payment is certain. In the base and wide cases only the low-rate branch pays. The wider model includes a negative low-node short rate, −2/247, which is admissible under the chapter's trading contract. All node gross bank returns remain positive.

For the base model, hold β units of the unit-face date-2 zero and x CU in the date-0 bank account. At date 1 sell the zeros, settle the bank position and pay the contract. Exact replication requires:

β(969/980)+x/(49/50) = 141/49,
β(19/20)+x/(49/50) = 0.
β = 1410/19; x = −69.09 CU.

Subtracting the equations solves β because the two successor bond prices differ. The borrowed 69.09 becomes a 70.50 date-1 repayment. The initial bond holding costs β(0.95) = 70.50, so the net initial cost is 1.41. Its two net date-1 payments are exactly 141/49 and zero. Borrowing and the ability to sell the bond at date 1 are essential trading rights here. If the two successor bond prices were equal, the system would lose rank; a claim with different branch payments could not be replicated with just these two assets. The s = 0 claim has equal payments and can be replicated entirely by depositing 0.92.

Now freeze the base β and borrowing while the wider model describes date-1 bond values. The low-branch hedge delivers 423/98, but the claim requires 236/49: the error is −1/2 CU. In the high branch the hedge delivers −141/98 CU against a zero payment. Its priced error is (49/50)(1/2)[−1/2−141/98] = −0.95, equal to 1.41−2.36. The frozen hedge is underfunded relative to the wide-model contract price. This is model error, not an arbitrage between two simultaneously valid quotes in one unchanged model.

Using the wide model consistently would give β = 1180/19, initial bank position −56.64 and initial cost 2.36. More dispersion changes the payment distribution, the replication coefficients and the required funding together. A curve fit alone cannot select between those possibilities.

Additional liquid contingent-claim prices could restrict s or a richer dynamics parameterization, provided their contractual terms and curve conventions agree. Even then, identification can be weak, several parameters can offset one another, and extrapolation remains a model choice. A fit to one set of instruments is not an independent test on that same set. Reserve distinct instruments or dates for evaluation; retain bid–ask uncertainty and failures instead of choosing only easy calibration targets.

7. A scenario must say what is held fixed

The sensitivity chapter differentiated prices with respect to specified yield or zero-curve coordinates. Here we use a different, explicit coordinate: the three discount points D1, D2, D3. In each scenario keep s = 0.02 and conditional ℚ fixed, change a supplied discount point, recalibrate every affected level, and revalue. These are alternative date-0 curves. They are not realized date-1 nodes and do not come with physical occurrence probabilities.

Worked example 4 — Recalibration, maturity exposure and a payoff boundary

First lower D2 from 0.95 to 0.94, keeping D1 = 0.98 and D3 = 0.91. The 5/5/105 bond falls by 5(−0.01) to 105.15. The recalibrated date-1 discounts become 2397/2450 and 47/50. The claim still pays only in the low-rate branch, and its price falls to 0.90, a change of −0.51. The date-2 level also changes because it must still fit D3; freezing it would fail the calibration contract.

Separately restore the base curve and lower D3 from 0.91 to 0.905. The fixed-payment bond falls by 105(−0.005) to 104.675. The date-1 discounts and the contingent claim remain unchanged, so its price stays 1.41. There is no date-3 exposure in its payment rule under this particular sequential calibration family.

With q = 1/2 and only the low branch paying:
C0 = [100D2(1+s)−96D1]/2.
∂C0/∂D2 = 50(1+s) = 51;   ∂C0/∂D1 = −48;   ∂C0/∂D3 = 0.

These local scenario derivatives apply only while that payoff region persists and the calibration family is held fixed. They are not the β = 1410/19 exposure to the future date-1 bond price in Worked example 3. Different variables, dates and maintained restrictions produce different hedge coefficients. A large bump can change which branches pay, invalidating the local formula; the full max payoff must then be repriced.

8. Separate fitting, forecasting and validation evidence

A usable term-structure study specifies the assets' currency, maturity, cash timing and credit/collateral status before selecting a model. It documents which prices were actually available at each calibration date and how missing maturities were treated. Rates from incompatible contracts do not become a default-free curve merely because they line up smoothly. The present one-curve frictionless model deliberately excludes those institutional complications.

Use cross-sectional price errors to assess fit to the chosen instruments. Use later outcomes, proper forecast loss functions and prespecified information sets to evaluate a physical transition model. Compare plausible dynamics while holding today's curve fixed to assess claim and hedge model risk. These evaluations answer different questions. A model can succeed at one and fail at another; exact arithmetic cannot establish that its probabilities are empirically credible.

Expectations estimates need additional identifying information and maintained assumptions. For example, a time series can help estimate persistence and innovation behavior, while surveys can provide noisy measures of beliefs. Neither should be treated as error-free truth. State which parameters are identified by which moments, report uncertainty, and examine whether the decision changes under alternatives. A decomposition with a near-zero fitting residual can still have a wide uncertainty interval for its expected-rate component.

The credit-risk chapter adds default and recovery to positive state-price valuation. The binomial replication chapter develops broader contingent-claim replication, and Brownian motion and Ito calculus supplies tools needed for continuous-time extensions. The finite arguments here stand on their own; continuous-time model names are not substitutes for those later derivations.

Reproduce the calibration and challenge its interpretation

Download the exact input contracts, standard-library program, complete rational output, four-file integrity manifest and instructions and input domains. Run the program offline. It returns all model levels, node discounts/rates, Arrow weights, zero and coupon prices, physical holding premiums, eight full paths, claim replicas, frozen-hedge errors, recalibrated scenarios and the separate finite mean-reversion case. Fractions are exact strings; there is no simulation seed or numerical root tolerance.

Change only the physical probabilities first: fitted prices and claim hedges must remain fixed while forecasts, path SDFs and expected returns change. Next set s to zero and confirm the bank-only replica; change ℚ and confirm that calibration is rerun; finally move a discount point far enough to change the claim's payoff region. The input contract rejects nonpositive discounts, zero-probability branches, an invalid shape, changed dates, nonfinite values and a physical mean-reversion path with a nonpositive gross rate. It allows negative rates above −1. The supplied checker independently enumerates paths and solves pricing identities; it does not establish empirical validity or certify every possible model extension.

Exercises

  1. Reconstruct an identified level. With the base curve, q = 1/2 and s = 0.02, derive a2, its shape-weighted sum and c2 without using the saved output. Price a different bond paying 3, 3 and 103 at dates 1, 2 and 3. Explain exactly which model choices the fitted c2 is conditional on.
  2. Recombination is not identical accumulated wealth. For the base tree, calculate bank wealth A2 on histories LH and HL, their separate date-0 state prices, and their conditional price-weight shares within the middle date-2 node. Compare with their ℚ probability shares. Also compare the normalized Arrow weight of the lowest date-2 node with its ℚ node probability. Explain why assigning a single bank value to the middle rate node fails.
  3. Change beliefs, keep the pricing model. Change only the date-0 physical high probability from 0.7 to 0.3. Find the physical expected date-1 short rate, the two-year zero's expected one-year simple return and its expected excess return. State which initial prices and forward rates change. Then explain why setting ℙ = ℚ would still not generally make the forward equal the expected next short rate.
  4. Prove the dynamic no-arbitrage claim. For finitely many nodes and finite predictable holdings, prove that a self-financing strategy in consistently priced assets has a ℚ-martingale discounted wealth process. Use it to exclude a zero-cost arbitrage. Identify where strict probability support and positive bank wealth enter. Give a one-period counterexample if a traded positive physical-state indicator is assigned zero pricing probability.
  5. A different contingent strike. Keep the base model but change the date-1 contract to max(100P(1;2)−97,0). Compute its two payments, price, units of the unit-face date-2 zero and date-0 bank position for exact replication. Show both branch equations and the initial funding identity. State the rank condition that made the solution possible.
  6. Calibration is not identification. Derive the level formula ct for any strictly positive shapes and positive conditional ℚ probabilities. Explain why it fits each supplied D and why the level is unique conditional on those choices. Use the s = 0 and s = 0.04 models to refute the claim that three fitted discount points uniquely determine the date-1 nonlinear contract price. Describe one extra kind of evidence for pricing dynamics and one for physical forecasts.
  7. A large bump crosses a payment boundary. Hold D1 = 0.98, D3 = 0.91, s = 0.02 and q = 1/2. Derive the D2 interval on which only the low branch pays under the original strike 96. Change D2 from 0.95 to 0.92. Compare the extrapolated local formula, the correctly recalibrated claim price and the 5/5/105 bond price. Explain the error and why there is no negative claim value.
  8. Derive finite mean reversion. Iterate the additive recursion with independent fair ±1 innovations to derive its n-step mean and variance. For θ = 0.02, φ = 1/2, σ = 0.01 and r0 = 0.08, enumerate the two-step rates and verify the formulas. Explain the φ = 1 boundary, the need to name the probability law and why this physical example does not establish a curve fit.
  9. Two different negative-rate boundaries. Calculate the wide tree's low date-1 short rate from d = 247/245. Explain its admissibility under the stated contract. Now add an unrestricted costless cash-storage asset returning one over that interval and construct a conditional arbitrage. Separately evaluate the down/up outputs of r′ = r+κ(θ−r)+σ√r ε at r = 0.0025, κ = 0.2, θ = 0.03 and σ = 0.3. What happens to the one-step mean if the negative output is clamped to zero? Distinguish positive gross returns from a nonnegative-rate state domain.
  10. Critique a term-premium research memo. A fictional memo says: “Our model fits three zero prices exactly. Therefore its pricing probabilities are physical probabilities, its forward is the expected future short rate, and the forward-minus-forecast residual is a uniquely measured pure term premium. Adding more daily observations always removes persistence bias. The exact fitted hedge needs no validation.” Evaluate all five claims. Use the dated Federal Reserve methodological source within its inspected scope, not as evidence about current rates. Design a concise validation plan that separates fit, expectations and hedge performance, and identifies at least two uncertainties.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. The first Arrow row is (0.49,0.49). Multiplying by date-1 discounts and branch probabilities gives a2 = (969/4000,19/40,931/4000). The middle entry adds both incoming histories: 969/4000+931/4000 = 19/40. Multiplying by (26/25,1,24/25) gives 47519/50000. Therefore c2 = (91/100)/(47519/50000) = 45500/47519, and its resulting date-3 weights sum to 0.91. The alternative bond price is 3(0.98)+3(0.95)+103(0.91) = 99.52 CU. The fitted level is conditional on the chosen positive shapes, q values, dates, earlier calibrated levels and traded curve. It is not an independently estimated rate volatility or physical forecast.

  2. For LH, the discounts earned before date 2 are 49/50 and 969/980; their product is 969/1000. Thus A2(LH) = 1000/969. For HL the product is (49/50)(19/20) = 931/1000, giving A2(HL) = 1000/931. Each path has ℚ probability 1/4, so its state price is respectively 969/4000 and 931/4000. Their sum is 19/40. Within that middle node, the price-weight shares are 51/100 and 49/100, while their ℚ probability shares are 1/2 and 1/2.

    The lowest node's normalized Arrow weight is (969/4000)/(19/20) = 51/200 = 0.255, versus ℚ probability 1/4. A rate node specifies the current rate and future law, not the path of previously earned rates. Replacing both middle histories' bank wealth by one common value destroys their individual discounted-probability identities. Aggregated Arrow weights remain valid because they sum the distinct path prices correctly.

  3. The new physical expected rate is (7/10)(11/969)+(3/10)(1/19) = 23/969 ≈ 2.37358%. The two-year zero's simple returns remain 2/49 and 0, so its expected return becomes (7/10)(2/49) = 1/35 ≈ 2.85714%. Subtracting the bank rate 1/49 gives 2/245 ≈ 0.81633 percentage points. All D values, fixed-payment prices, contingent-claim prices, calibrated rates and forwards are unchanged because their chosen pricing law has not changed.

    If p = q = 1/2, the expected short rate becomes 31/969 while the forward remains 3/95; their gap is −2/4845. Nonlinear averaging survives even when the probability laws coincide. In this equality-of-laws case the bond's one-period expected excess return is zero. Neither observation licenses treating every maturity's yield as a physical forecast.

  4. For each traded asset i, let Sit be its ex-payment value and Yit+1 its next distribution. The pricing recursion gives Eℚ[(Sit+1+Yit+1)/At+1|t] = Sit/At. Holdings hit chosen at t are measurable with respect to current information. Multiply by them and sum. Self-financing makes ΣhitSit equal current wealth and the next pre-rebalancing sum equal next wealth. Hence Eℚ[Wt+1/At+1|t] = Wt/At. Iteration yields expected terminal discounted wealth W0.

    For W0 = 0, a nonnegative terminal payoff positive on some positive-ℙ path would have positive ℚ expectation because the laws have the same strictly positive support and AT is positive. That contradicts the equality. Finite states and finite positions justify the expectations; unrestricted anticipation or an unpriced external asset would break the argument's premises.

    For a counterexample, take two physical states each with probability 1/2, a bank gross return of one, and pricing probabilities (1,0). Make the second-state indicator (0,1) traded at its assigned price zero. Buying it costs zero, never loses and pays one with physical probability 1/2. Thus it is an arbitrage. The word traded is essential: the example cannot establish an arbitrage in a market where that payoff is unavailable and unspanned.

  5. The low payment is 100(969/980)−97 = 92/49; the high payment is 0. The price is (49/50)(1/2)(92/49) = 0.92. Subtracting β(969/980)+x/(49/50) = 92/49 and β(19/20)+x/(49/50) = 0 yields β = 920/19. The date-1 bank repayment is β(19/20) = 46, so x = −45.08. Initial bond cost is 46 and net cost is 46−45.08 = 0.92. The high branch nets zero; in the low branch the bond's extra sale value is β[(969/980)−(19/20)] = 92/49. The nonzero difference between successor bond values gives a rank-two system with the bank. No physical probability was needed to solve it.

  6. At date t choose dt,j = ctht,j. Because the two transition probabilities sum to one, the total next Arrow weight is ctΣat,jht,j. Setting it equal to Dt+1 gives ct = Dt+1/Σat,jht,j. A positive numerator and denominator give a positive unique level. Recursing preserves earlier prices because an earlier maturity does not depend on later short rates. The result is conditional on shapes and q; neither was solved for by this equation.

    At s = 0, the date-1 bond values are both 95/98 and the contract is worth 0.92. At s = 0.04, those values are 247/245 and 228/245, and the contract is worth 2.36. Both models fit all three supplied zeros. This constructive counterexample refutes unique dynamics identification without relying on parameter counting alone. Other liquid contingent-claim prices can restrict pricing dispersion; dated historical transitions or carefully measured survey expectations can inform physical dynamics. Each source of evidence needs its own error model, availability discipline and validation.

  7. The low branch pays positively when 100D2(1+s)/D1 > 96, hence D2 > 392/425 ≈ 0.922353. The high branch is positive when D2 > 96D1/[100(1−s)] = 0.96. Thus only the low branch pays positively for 392/425 < D2 ≤ 0.96; at the upper endpoint the high payment is exactly zero. The differentiable one-positive-branch formula applies in the open interior; a perturbation through an endpoint requires changing regimes.

    The extrapolated formula gives 1.41+51(0.92−0.95) = −0.12. At 0.92 both max expressions are instead zero, so the correctly recalibrated claim price is 0. The fixed-payment bond becomes 5(0.98)+5(0.92)+105(0.91) = 105.05. The local derivative assumed one positive branch and was used outside that region. A nonnegative claim valued with positive state prices cannot have a negative price. The model contains the payment boundary explicitly; the linear extrapolation discarded it.

  8. Subtract θ and substitute recursively: rn−θ = φn(r0−θ)+σΣk=1nφn−kεk. Taking expectations removes the innovation sum. Its variance is σ²Σφ2(n−k), since each innovation has variance one and distinct innovations have zero covariance. For φ < 1 this geometric sum equals σ²(1−φ2n)/(1−φ²). This derivation supplies the claimed formulas and their independence condition.

    The four two-step rates are (0.02,0.04,0.03,0.05), each with probability 1/4. Their mean is 7/200 = 0.035. Deviations are −0.015, 0.005, −0.005 and 0.015; their average square is 1/8000 = 0.000125, also 0.01²(1+0.5²). The conditional mean after the first step is 0.05, not 0.035; the latter is the date-0 two-step forecast. At φ = 1, the mean is r0 and variance nσ², obtained from the finite sum rather than dividing by zero. The named probability law determines whether these are physical forecasts or pricing-law moments. The physical process alone has not supplied a SDF or a calibrated bond-price system.

  9. The wide low-node rate is 245/247−1 = −2/247 ≈ −0.80972%. Its gross return 245/247 is positive, so it is allowed in the stipulated bank/bond economy. If costless storage is added, then at that node borrow 1 CU, put it into storage and repay 245/247 CU one year later. The surplus is 2/247. Adopt this zero-cost strategy only upon reaching that node; it has no loss on other histories and a positive gain on a positive-probability event. The enlarged trading opportunity set makes the negative rate inconsistent with no-arbitrage.

    For the separate square-root step, r+κ(θ−r) = 0.008 and σ√r = 0.015. The two rates are −0.007 and 0.023; their mean is 0.008. Clamping the negative rate to zero produces (0,0.023), with mean 0.0115, an increase of 0.0035. The negative outcome still has a positive bank gross return 0.993, but it violates a model whose state must be nonnegative to take √r at the next step. Changing that state with a clamp changes the law. Positivity of gross returns and invariance of a nonnegative state domain are different conditions.

  10. The fit constrains three initial prices; it does not establish ℙ = ℚ or select a unique transition law. Even with equal laws the forward differs from the expected short rate through nonlinear averaging. A forward-minus-forecast residual depends on the model, horizon and convention; calling it a uniquely observed pure premium omits those restrictions. More frequent measurements of a persistent process do not automatically supply more independent long-run variation. An exact in-model hedge remains exposed to misspecified dynamics, instruments and trading rights.

    The dated Federal Reserve methodological discussion supports caution about expectations identification, persistence and the convention including convexity; it supplies no evidence about our synthetic coefficients or current market expectations. A good validation plan freezes data availability and instrument definitions, reports calibration residuals relative to quote uncertainty, evaluates physical forecasts on later unused dates, compares several calibrated dynamics, and tests funded hedge errors on contracts outside the fitting sample. Report parameter uncertainty, observation error, model-family dependence and execution restrictions as applicable.

    Grade each of the five claims separately: require its missing assumption or counterexample, then require distinct tests for prices, forecasts and hedges, at least two concrete uncertainties, and accurate source scope/date. Plausible alternative designs earn full credit when their identifying logic is explicit. Merely attaching a source link or proposing a larger sample does not answer the identification question.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a treasury committee why two models can fit every supplied zero and still disagree about a contingent price and its hedge. Benchmark answer: zeros constrain average discounted unit payments at specified dates. Their fit leaves the distribution of future bond prices open. A nonlinear payment responds to that distribution, so its price and replicating holdings can differ. Demonstrate 0.92 versus 2.36 from the common curve, name the trading rights behind replication, and distinguish physical forecast evidence from additional pricing instruments. An explanation that says only “models differ” has not shown the mechanism.

Delayed check. In the base model change only date-0 p to 1/2. Answer: the expected next short rate is 31/969, still above forward 3/95 by 2/4845; the two-year zero's expected one-year excess return is 0; its price and the contingent price stay 0.95 and 1.41. Separately restore p and change only D3 to 0.90, recalibrating with s and ℚ fixed. Answer: the 5/5/105 bond is 104.15, a fall of 1.05, while the date-1 contingent claim remains 1.41. Neither curve scenario has an implied physical occurrence probability.

Scope and deeper study

This chapter proves finite dynamically consistent valuation, positive-state-price no-arbitrage, conditional calibration and elementary replication under its trading contract. It derives finite mean reversion and exhibits pricing-law, physical-law and nonlinear-averaging distinctions. It does not estimate a real yield curve, establish a unique market term premium, fit a continuous-time short-rate model or guarantee an implementable hedge outside the stated market. Multi-factor dynamics, stochastic volatility, collateral-specific curves, measurement error and continuous-time estimation require additional methods and evidence.

The scoped methodological routes are the accepted finite pricing lecture, Haugh's selected lattice sections and the dated Federal Reserve model Q&A. Their inspected scope is recorded separately. Every numerical curve, tree, payment, exercise and scenario here is original. Passing the lab establishes reproducibility of these conditional calculations; choosing a model for actual decisions remains an empirical and governance task.

Sources and further study

  • Markus K. Brunnermeier — FIN 501 Lecture 03: One-Period Model, Pricing — Primary teaching route for linear payoff pricing, strictly positive finite-state prices, completeness and risk-neutral/SDF representations. Aster examples, exercises and the projection proof are original.
  • Martin Haugh — Term Structure Lattice Models (IEOR E4706 Foundations of Financial Engineering, 2016) — Finite-lattice teaching route for dated short-rate discounting, backward bond valuation, forward Arrow prices and sequential calibration; selected additive versus log-rate lattice comparisons. The discount-shape calibration, numbers and every example here are original.
  • Federal Reserve Board — Three-Factor Nominal Term Structure Model: methodological Q&A (updated 5 November 2019) — Dated methodological distinction between fitted yields, physical expectations and a convention for term premiums that includes convexity; persistence, finite-history and survey-information limits on expectations estimation. No current market estimate is used.
